newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice Dept. supports assisted-suicide ban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice Dept. supports assisted-suicide ban.

text.p: The Clinton administration strongly urged the Supreme Court Tuesday to declare that states may constitutionally ban doctor-assisted suicide.

In potential landmark cases from New York and Washington state, administration lawyers drew a distinction between a doctor who simply allows a terminally ill patient to die and and one who helps a patient take his or her own life.

"A state legislature ... may conclude that extremely important state interests justify a distinction between the refusal of unwanted medical treatment and the prescription of lethal dosages of medication for the purpose of ending life," Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said.

He argued that the state's interests include preventing the deaths of patients erroneously diagnosed as terminally ill and "prohibiting a practice that is vulnerable to abuse or error and extremely difficult to police."

Dellinger, the administration's chief lawyer before the high court, rejected the view that the so-called right-to-die was similar to a woman's constitutional right to an abortion. "The right to choose an abortion implicates a constellation of liberty and equality rights of fundamental importance that are not implicated here," he said.
He warned of dangers in doctor-assisted suicide. "Once a state decides to create an exception to its prohibition against assisted suicide, there is no obvious stopping point."

He also expressed concern about the possible deaths of people who are not competent or terminally ill and who are steered toward taking their lives by family members exhausted by their illness, by fears of being a "burden" or by doctors who fail to offer them continued support.
"The state has an interest of the highest order in prohibiting its physicians from assisting in the purposeful taking of another person's life," Dellinger concluded.

His argument reflected the views of President Clinton, who has said repeatedly since his 1992 campaign that he does not support a right to doctor-assisted suicide, which more than 30 states have made a crime.

Advocates say mentally competent, terminally ill patients should be able to seek help from their doctors when they believe the time has come to end their suffering. Opponents believe doctors should not be in the business of ending lives and that when a patient's pain and depression are treated the desire for death often fades.
The American Medical Association, the leading U.S. doctors' organisation, and more than 30 other health care groups have filed briefs opposing physician-assisted suicide.

"The real issue for us is that if they want suicide, don't ask physicians to be the participants. We don't think it is ethical. We are about healing patients," Dr. Tom Reardon, vice chairman of the AMA board of trustees, said in a telephone interview.

Entering a divisive social debate that approaches the controversy over abortion and capital punishment in emotional intensity, the high court has agreed to decide in its 1996-97 term whether states may ban doctor-assisted suicide. Arguments are expected in January with a decision due by summer.

The Justice Department and AMA are urging the Supreme Court to overturn two precedent-setting lower-court rulings that struck down as unconstitutional laws from New York and Washington against doctor-assisted suicide.
The cases before the Supreme Court do not involve retired pathologist Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the best-known U.S. advocate of assisted suicide, who has assisted in more than 40 cases.

The Supreme Court last addressed a related issue in 1990, ruling that a person has a constitutional right to refuse unwanted medical treatment in a case involving a comatose woman whose parents wanted to end artifical life support.
